title: Former Red Deer, Alta., mayor seriously hurt in hit and run with e-bike or e-scooter calls for stricter rules
summary: Former Red Deer mayor Ken Johnston is calling for changes to e-bike and e-scooter rules in the central Alberta city after he was seriously injured by one of the vehicles in what police are calling a…

image.caption: Ken Johnston at the Red Deer Regional Hospital Centre’s trauma centre on Nov. 3, 2026. Johnston served as Red Deer’s mayor from 2021 to 2025 and was a city councillor before that. (Submitted by Tamaran Johnston)

blocks.text: Edmonton

Former Red Deer mayor Ken Johnston is calling for changes to e-bike and e-scooter rules in the central Alberta city after he was seriously injured by one of the vehicles in what police are calling a hit and run.
Ken Johnston served as Red Deer’s mayor from 2021 to 2025
“We have to make some changes here, that's for sure,” he told CBC News in an interview on Monday.
Johnston served as Red Deer’s mayor from 2021 to 2025 and was a city councillor before that.
“We're all in a state of shock,” daughter Tamaran Johnston told CBC News. “That somebody could leave a 72-year-old man alone on the sidewalk unconscious is just unfathomable to any of us.
“I don't know how anybody can leave anybody alone like that without checking to see if they're OK.”
In a news release Monday, the RCMP said they are asking for tips from the public as they investigate what happened and to identify a suspect.

Police said at about 7 a.m. on Nov. 3, officers were called to a hit-and-run crash involving an e-scooter or e-bike and a pedestrian at the intersection of 30th Avenue and McLean Street. They said the pedestrian sustained serious but non-life-threatening injuries and was taken to hospital.

In an interview with CBC News, Johnston recounted what happened. He said he was on his daily morning walk when an e-bike or e-scooter struck him from behind, knocking him unconscious and leaving him with multiple injuries.
“There's a very patchy, very fragmented memory of the whole thing,” he said. “I have no recollection of even the state of myself.”
Tamaran said she rushed to the hospital’s trauma centre after her family learned what happened to her father.
“His face had taken the brunt of the fall," she said, adding her father suffered multiple facial fractures and three lumbar spine fractures.
An undated file photo of Tamaran Johnston and her father Ken Johnston, the former mayor of Red Deer. (Submitted by Tamaran Johnston)
Tamaran said her father is now recovering at home, although the family remains shaken.
She said she wants to see stricter e-bike and e-scooter rules in Red Deer and that she hopes changes are made before next summer.
E-vehicle market evolves
Ken Johnston said the e-vehicle market has changed since Red Deer city council first introduced its regulated e-scooter program in 2017.
“That was a very segmented market,” he said.
“It was a seniors market. It was designed to keep people like me still able to ride their bicycle.”

In recent years, Johnston added, the market has expanded and now allows for youths as young as 12 to legally ride e-bikes. He said he believes the e-vehicles have a “destructive capability” and that perhaps more needs to be done to ensure that riders are qualified to use them responsibly.

items: ‘A bit of a dog’s breakfast’: Red Deer mayor wants province-wide rules for e-scooters

blocks.text: In a statement to CBC News, Red Deer RCMP said officers have noticed an increase in the use of electric modes of transportation in the city.

Red Deer Mayor Cindy Jefferies said that while commercial companies like Lime are regulated and that their vehicles are used responsibly for the most part, a wave of privately owned devices has changed the landscape.

“I think it's hit us — in a way — very fast and [we] probably didn't see the numbers of privately owned e-mobility devices coming forward,” she said, pointing to e-scooters and electric dirt bikes of varying sizes and speeds.
"There is obviously a very real need to regulate and restrict where they are [and] how fast they can be going.”

At the Alberta Municipalities convention in September, Jefferies said Red Deer supported a resolution urging the provincial government to introduce uniform regulations and enforcement tools across Alberta.

In a statement to CBC News, a spokesperson for the Ministry of Transportation and Economic Corridors said Alberta is pursuing legislative amendments to the Traffic Safety Act to modernize the system and support different road users.

“As part of these amendments, Alberta is considering a provincial framework to support the safe and consistent use of personal micromobility devices, such as e-scooters and similar small devices, where municipalities enforce and choose to allow them,” the spokesperson said.
Provincial action needed, mayor says
Jefferies said she believes provincewide consistency is key so that rules and safety requirements don't change from one community to the next.
While e-bikes and e-scooters offer a valuable option for people who don't own a car or who rely on transit, Jefferies said they create enforcement challenges.
“How do we get a playing field, if you will, where everyone knows the rules and everyone understands and abides by those rules.”

items: Alberta gov't mulling regulations around micromobility vehicles like e-scooters

blocks.text: Jefferies said as Red Deer waits to see how the province responds to these concerns, city council is looking at what other options it has to address them, such as giving enforcement officers stronger tools.
She also urged riders to understand the risks involved to them as well as pedestrians.
"People don't understand that there's a real risk, there's danger and that these [e-vehicles] are pretty powerful."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Nadeer Hashmi is a reporter for CBC News in Red Deer, Alta. He was formerly a reporter in Yellowknife.
